# Camera eyes {#sec-camera-eyes}

<div data-life="status" data-stage="2.1"></div>

Chapter 1 ended with an animal that steers, avoids what hurts, learns which food to distrust, looks after two
needs and carries a mood for a while. It did all of that with five coarse eyes. This chapter builds the brain of
an early fish on top of it, and a fish sees far better than a worm. So the first step of the chapter is not a new
part of the brain. It is better eyes, and a world to use them in.

## The world of this chapter

The last stage of chapter 1 grew every kind of bush in its own patches. That gave the two lasting states their
job, and it took the job away from learning: in a patch of one kind, the first bite says everything about the
neighbours. The stages of this chapter are about learning, so they need a world in which learning pays.

Several worlds were tried with the animals of chapter 1. Patches that were mostly one kind, with some poison
standing between the good bushes, did not bring learning back, however the kinds were mixed. Only a world without
patches did, where good and poison bushes stand side by side everywhere. That is the world of this chapter. It is
the cold world of the drives stage, with more bushes and more room.

The price is that the two lasting states of the previous stage have less to do here. That is accepted. Not every
part of a brain matters equally in every place.

The food is as before: four kinds of berry bush, new in every life, half of them poison.

<div data-life="settings" data-stage="2.1"></div>

## The biology: an eye that forms an image

The eyes of early bilaterians were little more than light-sensitive spots that told bright from dark and one side
from the other. Vertebrates have camera eyes: a lens throws an image onto a sheet of receptors, and the brain
receives many small views side by side. With the image came a part of the midbrain that holds a map of it, the
*optic tectum*. In a fish or a frog the tectum picks out something small and moving, turns the eyes and body to
it, and starts the escape from something large that grows quickly.

This stage gives the animal the sharper eyes and leaves the tectum out. In this world nothing moves and nothing
hunts, so the quick, inborn reactions that the tectum is known for have nothing to react to. A first design, a map
that picked the nearest thing in view and steered to it, was tried before any evolution and did not help: the
animal already steers to bushes with the reflexes it evolved in chapter 1, and "the nearest thing" is as often an
empty bush or a poison one. The other thing a tectum does, letting what the animal has learned choose where to
turn, needs the parts of the brain that this chapter adds later.

## The change

The animal now looks in nine directions where it had five, and sees one step further.

No cells are added. Every part of the brain that listened to the five old eyes now listens to all nine, and every
connection from every eye is its own: there is no copy of a circuit per eye, and nothing forces two eyes to mean
the same. What a look is worth, and in which direction it counts, is for evolution and for the animal's own
learning to settle, eye by eye.

The four new eyes sit between the old ones. They do not start silent. Each new connection starts as the average
of the same connection from the two neighbouring eyes, so that the animal makes sense of what the new eyes see
from its first tick. Nine eyes send nearly twice as much as five, which would overwhelm the cells that listen, so
all connections from the eyes are made weaker by the same factor.

<div data-life="brain" data-stage="2.1"></div>

## Results

### The run

This stage has no control. Its question is not whether a new circuit earns its place, but whether the animals of
chapter 1 settle into the new world with their new eyes. The comparison is with the population they started from.

<div data-life="curves" data-stage="2.1"></div>

<div data-life="summary" data-stage="2.1"></div>

The curve of a run is hard to read here, because every generation lives in a new world and the worlds differ a
great deal. The fair comparison puts the starting population and the evolved one in the same worlds. That is the
table below, in the row for this stage's world: the evolved animals do clearly better than the ones they
descend from.

<div data-life="table" data-stage="2.1" data-example="crowding"></div>

### Room

The same table shows why the world was made larger. With the same animals and the same density of bushes, both
populations do better when there is more room, and the better population gains the most.

The reason is in what is left standing. A good bush is emptied in a few bites. A poison bush loses one berry and
keeps the rest. Where many animals forage close together, the bushes that still carry berries are more and more
the poison ones, and the good ones run out nearby although the world as a whole grows plenty. A population that
forages better does this to itself faster. In a small world that hides part of an improvement, so the world of
this chapter has twice the area of the worlds of chapter 1.

### Is learning used again?

<div data-life="lesions" data-stage="2.1"></div>

Yes, and more than at any point in chapter 1. With learning switched off, the animals lose about half of their
fitness and eat far more poison. In the patches of the previous stage the same switch cost nothing.

The new eyes have a part in that. The lesson of a poison bite is written into the connections from every eye, so
nine eyes carry it where five did, and the animal recognises the poison from more directions.

The two lasting states of the previous stage, `flee` and the chain from `fed` to `settle`, matter little in this
world, as expected without patches. They stay in the brain.

When the four new eyes started silent instead, the animals did worse after the same number of generations, and
the new eyes were still weak at the end. Evolution alone needs a long time to give dozens of new connections per
cell a meaning; copying the neighbours gives it something to adjust.

### How a life is spent

<div data-life="table" data-stage="2.1" data-example="life_spent"></div>

These animals find food almost at once, and most of them still die young. What kills them is not hunger but
poison: an animal bites the same kinds of poison bush again and again, far more often than it would need to find
out which ones they are, and a few bites cost as much as the stomach it was born with. When it does eat well, it
keeps biting on a full stomach, which gains nothing and strips the good bushes around it.

Both are failures of learning, and they set the task for the stages that follow: to tell apart things that look
alike, to remember what was learned about each, and to learn what is worth wanting and not only what to avoid.
